title: HLD interview framework & rubric
relevance: High — the pacing/structure and scoring lens for every 45-min “design X” HLD round (campus + experienced); FAANG and Indian product cos (Atlassian, Uber, Flipkart, etc.) grade how you run requirements → architecture → deep dives → tradeoffs, not a memorized diagram alone.
company_notes: Campus/early-career India product cos (Flipkart, Uber, Atlassian, etc.) often run one HLD-style or lighter design-at-scale discussion after coding and still expect clarify → diagram → bottlenecks; FAANG/big-tech mid+ typically a 45–60 min HLD with delivery and tradeoff depth (new-grad loops may skip or shorten); this framework is meta for every later HLD question.

phases.goal: Establish that a 45-min HLD round grades process, judgment, and collaboration—not a memorized “correct” diagram.

must_hit.point: Candidate leads a 45-min design conversation; the interviewer grades process and judgment under time, not a unique correct diagram.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says they own pacing, announce phases, and expect redirects—not a single right architecture.

must_hit.point: FRs are “users can…” capabilities (top 3 features); NFRs are quantified qualities, not vague “highly available / fast / secure.”
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives concrete FR wording and quantified NFR examples like feed p99 < 200ms or availability-over-consistency on a timeline.

must_hit.point: Exponent-style scoring covers requirements, design+tradeoffs, scalability/performance, fault tolerance/reliability, and communication/collaboration (weak → very strong maps to hire advocacy).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists those five buckets and ties weak/strong ratings to how interviewers advocate hire vs no-hire.

probes: What is the interviewer actually grading in a 45-min design-X HLD round?
How do you distinguish a strong FR/NFR set from a weak one?

hints.1: Think process and scoring lens, not a diagram you memorized.
hints.2: Separate what users can do from quantified system qualities, then name the rubric buckets.
hints.3: Lead the 45-min convo; FRs = top 3 “users can…”; NFRs quantified; score requirements, design+tradeoffs, scale/perf, fault tolerance, and communication.

phases.goal: Lock the merged 45-min skeleton: time-boxed requirements → entities → API → simple HLD → deep dives → wrap, with working path before complexity.

must_hit.point: Merged skeleton: FR+NFR+out-of-scope (~5) → core entities (~2) → API/interface (~5) → simple HLD for FRs (~10–15) → deep dives on NFRs/bottlenecks (~10) → wrap (~3–5).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Walks the phases in order with those time boxes and mentions announcing them so the interviewer can pace/redirect.

must_hit.point: Working system first: complete path for core APIs before caches, queues, or shards; unfinished HLD is the #1 mid-level fail.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Draws happy-path boxes/arrows for every core API, notes “add cache later,” and refuses to stall on one box.

must_hit.point: Optional early estimation only if numbers change the design; otherwise estimate the crux in the deep dive—avoid ritual QPS theater.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States when they would skip upfront math vs when sharding/cache/replication depends on a crux number.

must_hit.point: Deep dive signals seniority: juniors follow probes; senior+ self-pick 1–2 hard spots (hot read path, write fan-out, consistency edge, SPOF) and drive tradeoffs.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names 1–2 bottleneck spots from their HLD and starts option A vs B without waiting to be asked.

probes: Walk me through how you’d spend a 45-min HLD round minute by minute.
When do you estimate, and what must be on the board before Redis/Kafka/sharding?

hints.1: Start from Hello Interview’s delivery pacing, then merge the wrap.
hints.2: Time-box requirements and API, then a complete FR path before scale toys; estimate only if it changes architecture class.
hints.3: ~5 reqs → ~2 entities → ~5 API → ~10–15 simple HLD → ~10 deep dives → ~3–5 wrap; working path first; senior+ pick 1–2 hard spots.

phases.goal: Show justified alternatives for major choices, plus ops/cost/failure signal and collaborative buy-in—not buzzword drops.

must_hit.point: Tradeoff language wins: name rejected alternatives (SQL vs NoSQL, fan-out-on-write vs read, sync vs async) and why for this NFR; naming Kafka/Redis without a reason is a red flag.
must_hit.evidence_hint: For each major choice, states option rejected, option chosen, and the NFR that decided it.

must_hit.point: Ops/cost are no longer optional: mention failure modes + mitigation, monitoring/alerts, and rough cost/right-sizing when relevant.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Unprompted, ties a component failure to user impact, mitigation, and a monitoring or cost note.

must_hit.point: Collaborate, don’t monologue: check in after HLD for buy-in, leave room for deep-dive probes, absorb hints.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Pauses after HLD to ask if the shape looks right and invites the interviewer into the deep dive.

probes: You chose that store/queue—what did you reject and why for these NFRs?
What happens if this component dies, and how would you know in production?

hints.1: Every major box needs an alternative you considered.
hints.2: Tie the choice to a named NFR, then add failure impact and how you’d watch it.
hints.3: State A vs B + NFR reason; cover SPOF/mitigation/monitoring/cost; ask for buy-in after HLD.

phases.goal: Apply the framework under timers: distill requirements, gate estimation, map APIs, HLD happy path, then deep-dive and wrap.

must_hit.point: Requirements drill: for a prompt like Design Instagram, produce ≤3 FRs + ≤4 quantified NFRs, mark out-of-scope, and confirm with the interviewer (about a 5–7 min box).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Stops with a short confirmed FR/NFR/out-of-scope list instead of feature sprawl or vague adjectives.

must_hit.point: HLD-only discipline: map each FR to 1–2 APIs/events first; then ~12 min boxes/arrows for happy path only—no Redis/Kafka/sharding until every FR has a path.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Shows API contract on the board, then narrates data/state through a complete simple HLD before scale components.

must_hit.point: Full timed dry run ends with a 60-sec wrap: design summary, top tradeoffs, and what you’d improve with more time; leave ≥10 min for deep dives.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Protects deep-dive time, picks weakest NFR spots + SPOF with A vs B, and closes in about a minute.

probes: Design Instagram—run only the requirements script, then tell me if you’d estimate before HLD.
You have about 12 minutes—draw the happy-path HLD for your APIs with no cache or queue yet.

hints.1: Treat this as a timed script, not a feature brainstorm.
hints.2: Confirm ≤3 FRs and ≤4 NFRs; APIs before boxes; forbid scale toys until paths exist.
hints.3: 5–7 min requirements → APIs → 12 min simple HLD → ≥10 min deep dives → 60-sec wrap of summary, tradeoffs, next steps.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Do capacity math only when numbers change architecture class (sharding/cache/replication); otherwise skip ritual DAU→QPS theater and estimate the crux during deep dive.

tradeoffs.topic: Simple working HLD vs early microservices/Kafka/cache
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Draw a complete monolith-style path that satisfies FRs first; introduce async, cache, or split services as deep-dive upgrades tied to specific NFRs—not as the opening diagram.

tradeoffs.topic: SQL vs NoSQL (and similar store choices)
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Name both options and pick from this problem’s NFRs (consistency, access pattern, scale lever)—never “NoSQL scales better” without peak QPS, read/write ratio, and a concrete lever.
State both, map to write amplification vs read latency/cost for this workload, and say which NFR wins.
Sync when the user path needs the result now; async when NFRs allow eventual work (queues) and you can describe failure/retry behavior.

gotchas.trap: Estimating first every time because it feels expected.
gotchas.correction: Numbers only when they pick architecture class; ritual DAU→QPS ending in “so… it’s a lot” wastes signal.

gotchas.trap: Jumping to microservices, Kafka, or Redis before a working HLD.
gotchas.correction: Over-engineering; simple path first, then async/cache as deep-dive upgrades tied to NFRs.

gotchas.trap: Making a major design choice with no alternatives or “why.”
gotchas.correction: Every major choice needs a rejected alternative and an NFR reason—silence tanks the technical-design rubric bucket.

gotchas.trap: Saying a component “is replicated” as fault tolerance.
gotchas.correction: Cover SPOF, redundancy, retries/backoff, degraded mode, and user impact plus mitigation.

gotchas.trap: Burning the round on schema/requirements and starving deep dives.
gotchas.correction: Time-box requirements (~5) and HLD; leave ≥10 min for deep dives; schema fields that don’t drive design are noise.

gotchas.trap: Claiming scale with vague “NoSQL scales better.”
gotchas.correction: Tie to peak QPS, read/write ratio, and a concrete lever (replicas, shard key, cache, CDN, queue).
